newsitem.title: SWEDEN: Crew of Estonia ferry to be criticised in report.
newsitem.headline: Crew of Estonia ferry to be criticised in report.

text.p: The crew of the Estonia ferry that sank in 1994 with the loss of 852 lives will be heavily criticised in a final report by a three-nation investigation committee, a Swedish paper said on Thursday.
The daily paper Dagens Nyheter said the report would confirm a preliminary finding that poor design of the ferry's bow visor was at fault for the disaster in September 1994.

The visor, which lifts up and down to allow cars on and off, was ripped off during a storm in the Baltic as the ferry sailed from the Estonian capital of Tallinn to Stockholm. Water flooded onto the deck, destabilising the ship which sank.
But commission sources told Dagens Nyheter that the committee also found that the mainly Estonian crew made several mistakes on the fateful night.

The ship was poorly loaded in Tallinn and the crew was forced to fill the port stabilising tank before departure to right the ship. This meant that the sudden heeling over could never be corrected, Dagens Nyheter said.

Officers on the bridge never checked the monitor, which showed the car deck, in the map room next to them, the newspaper report said. Two of the machine crew members saw on the monitor that water entered the car deck but did not notify the bridge.

It said the automatic speed pilot was on during the entire trip, possibly increasing the strain on the bow visor. The passenger alarm came late and not in a language everybody could understand, it said, while the Mayday signal to surrounding ships were sent too late.
The Estonian chairman of the committee, Uno Laur, had said last month that the crew did not make any serious mistakes but were a few minutes slow in sounding emergency alarms.
Only around 100 people survived the disaster. In total, 501 Swedes, 280 Estonians, 22 Latvians, 10 Finns, 12 Russians, six Norwegians and 21 people from 10 other countries were killed.
The official report of the commission, made up of Estonian, Swedish and Finnish maritime officials, has been delayed several times but is now expected to be released in the next few months.
